title: Bowl with Arabic Inscription, "Blessing, Prosperity, Well-being, Happiness"
medium: Earthenware; white slip with polychrome slip decoration under transparent glaze

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1940
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A wide, shallow ceramic bowl seen from above. Its decoration is a ring of Arabic lettering with tall, stretched vertical strokes, set around a central pattern of interlacing bands.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, date, medium, country, credit line, public-domain flag, tags (Arabic) and image URLs read from the record; museum page text read for the inscription and decoration

context: This earthenware bowl was made in what is now Uzbekistan, probably in Samarqand according to the Met, and was excavated at Nishapur in Iran. Its main decoration is Arabic calligraphy, a type of pottery often called epigraphic ware, painted in colored slip under a clear glaze.

descriptions.k: This is a big bowl. Its main decoration is writing! Look at the tall, stretched letters that march around the bowl. A crossing pattern sits in the middle. Can you trace one letter with your finger in the air?
descriptions.g12: Long ago, a potter in Central Asia made this bowl and painted words on it. The writing is Arabic, and it is the decoration. Some letters are stretched tall on purpose, so the line looks balanced. A woven-looking pattern sits in the middle. Follow the letters with your eyes like a path.
descriptions.g35: This clay bowl was made about a thousand years ago in what is now Uzbekistan. It has no animals or people on it. Its decoration is Arabic writing, a message of good wishes for its owner, spread around the inside in careful lettering. The Met notes that the tall vertical strokes were probably added to make the line look more harmonious. In the center, crossing bands form a knot-like pattern. How can letters be both words and design?
descriptions.g68: Potters in the Samanid-era world of Central Asia often decorated bowls with calligraphy alone, using blessings or proverbs. This one was probably made in Samarqand and was found at Nishapur in Iran, which shows how far pottery could travel. The letters are painted in slip, a liquid clay, beneath a clear glaze. Notice how the stretched vertical strokes create rhythm and how the central interlace anchors the whole design. Why might a message of good wishes suit an everyday vessel?
descriptions.g910: This bowl shows how calligraphy can serve as a complete decorative program. The Arabic text, a blessing for the owner, is the principal ornament. The museum notes that the tall vertical strokes were probably extended to make the inscription look more harmonious, and that the wording appears to be unique. A central motif of interlaced straps, which the Met links to Samarqand metalwork, balances the lettering. Consider how legibility, rhythm, and pattern compete and cooperate across the curved surface.
descriptions.g1112: Samanid-era epigraphic ware raises questions about the boundary between writing and ornament. Here a short Arabic blessing becomes rhythm: elongated verticals may serve visual harmony more than easy reading, and the museum observes that one word is cut short, which may suggest design sometimes outranked complete spelling. The central interlace, comparable to motifs on metal objects from Samarqand, hints at exchange between media. Made in present-day Uzbekistan yet excavated at Nishapur, the bowl also invites reflection on trade, though how it traveled and who used it remain open.

k.daily: Writing is the picture on this bowl. Can you find the tallest letter strokes? Point to three.
k.emotion: If this bowl could say a happy message, how would it make you feel? Why?
k.observation: Look all the way around the bowl. What do you see in the middle, and what do you see around the edge?
k.analysis: Where do your eyes start looking on this bowl? Where do they go next?
k.line: Some lines on this bowl go up tall. Can you draw a tall line in the air like the letters?
k.shape: The middle of the bowl has a crossing pattern. What shapes can you find in it?
k.color: How many colors can you count on the bowl? Which one do you see most?
k.texture: The bowl has a shiny clear glaze on top. How do you think it would feel under your fingers?
k.space: This bowl is wide and low, like a big dish. What could you put inside it?
k.light: The glaze can make a bowl shine when light touches it. Which parts might sparkle?
k.meaning: The words on this bowl are kind wishes. What kind wish would you paint on a bowl?
k.culture: People made this bowl a very long time ago, far from here. How is it like a bowl in your kitchen?
k.technique: The potter painted the letters with runny clay before the clear glaze went on. Why might that be a tricky way to paint?
k.personal: If you could decorate a bowl with your name, how would you make the letters look?
k.critical: Is this a picture or is it writing? What makes you think so?

g12.daily: The letters on this bowl are the main decoration. Which letters seem the tallest, and why might the potter stretch them?
g12.emotion: The words on the bowl are good wishes. How does that change how you feel about the bowl?
g12.observation: Describe the bowl from the middle to the rim. What do you see in each part?
g12.analysis: How do the tall letter strokes and the center pattern balance each other?
g12.line: Some strokes go straight up and some curve along the bowl. Which kind of line do you like better here?
g12.shape: Look at the crossing bands in the middle. How many different shapes can you find where they cross?
g12.color: Which colors in the letters and pattern pop out against the pale background?
g12.texture: The painted letters sit under a glossy glaze. How would that surface feel compared with raw clay?
g12.space: The bowl curves up and out. How does a round bowl change the way we see lines of writing?
g12.light: Imagine a lamp shining across this bowl. Where would the glaze look brightest?
g12.meaning: The Met says the words wish the owner blessing and happiness. Why would someone put wishes on a bowl?
g12.culture: This bowl was made in Central Asia a thousand years ago. What does a bowl with writing on it tell you about the people who made it?
g12.technique: The potter used slip, which is runny clay, like paint. What would be hard about painting tall, even letters with it?
g12.personal: What message would you put around a bowl for a friend?
g12.critical: Can you tell what the letters say just by looking? What does that teach us about writing in different languages?

g35.daily: This bowl uses Arabic writing as its main decoration instead of pictures. What makes the writing work as art?
g35.emotion: How does a bowl made to carry good wishes feel different from a bowl decorated with a scary or silly picture?
g35.observation: Spend one minute looking only at the lettering. What do you notice about the heights and spacing of the strokes?
g35.analysis: How does the potter organize the writing around the bowl so that it feels balanced?
g35.line: Compare the tall, straight strokes with the curving connecting lines. How do they work together in a line of writing?
g35.shape: How do the circle of the bowl, the ring of letters, and the central knot shape repeat or answer each other?
g35.color: How does the color of the lettering stand out from the white slip behind it?
g35.texture: How does the smooth, glassy glaze change how you see the painted letters underneath?
g35.space: The writing wraps around a curved, hollow form. How might the design look different on a flat wall?
g35.light: Glaze makes a surface reflect light. How might the bowl look different in a dim room and in bright sun?
g35.meaning: The Met says this wording of good wishes seems to be unique. Why might a potter want a one-of-a-kind message?
g35.culture: The bowl was made in present-day Uzbekistan but found in Nishapur, Iran. What might that tell you about travel and trade?
g35.technique: Slip is a mixture of clay and water used like paint. What skills would a potter need to write evenly with it?
g35.personal: Think of a phrase that is special to you. How would you lay it out around a bowl?
g35.critical: The bowl has only writing, no people or animals. What might be the benefits of decorating with words alone?

g68.daily: How does this bowl turn a spoken wish into a visual pattern that you can enjoy without reading it?
g68.emotion: What mood do the steady rhythm of the letters and the calm central knot create? Which choices build it?
g68.observation: List the parts of the design from rim to center. Which are writing and which are pattern?
g68.analysis: How does the central interlace balance the ring of calligraphy? What would change if it were missing?
g68.line: How does the potter vary vertical and horizontal strokes to create rhythm? Where does the rhythm feel strongest?
g68.shape: How do the tall verticals interrupt the curved shape of the bowl, and why might that be effective?
g68.color: How does the contrast between the white slip ground and the painted forms on it make the lettering readable?
g68.texture: How do you think the matte painted slip and the clear glaze above it affect the surface you see?
g68.space: How does the ring of writing guide the eye around the curved interior and toward the center?
g68.light: Where might a glazed, curved surface catch highlights, and how would those highlights change as the bowl is turned?
g68.meaning: An inscription can be both a message and a decoration. Which role do you think is more important here, and why?
g68.culture: Why might a blessing be a popular decoration on dishes in the Samanid-era world, and what does it suggest about hospitality?
g68.technique: Painting letters in slip under a glaze means mistakes are hard to fix. How might that shape the potter's approach?
g68.personal: When have you seen writing used as decoration on something you own? How was it different from this?
g68.critical: The museum says one word is cut short and that tall strokes may be for harmony. What does that suggest about the priority of design over legibility?

g910.daily: How does this bowl fuse language and ornament so completely that reading and looking become the same act?
g910.emotion: How can an inscription of good wishes shape a viewer's emotional response even before it is read?
g910.observation: Describe the visual hierarchy of the bowl, from the lettering to the central motif. What gets attention first?
g910.analysis: Analyze how the elongated verticals create the rhythm of the inscription and how the central interlace answers it.
g910.line: How does the potter's control of stroke height and spacing turn simple letters into a decorative frieze?
g910.shape: How does the radial organization of the design respond to the circular, concave form of the bowl?
g910.color: How does polychrome slip against a white ground create emphasis and unity without any pictorial subject?
g910.texture: How would the transition from painted slip to glassy glaze affect the way a viewer reads depth on this surface?
g910.space: What does the writing's placement on the inside of a vessel suggest about when and how the design was meant to be seen?
g910.light: How might the reflective glaze complicate or enhance the reading of the painted forms from different viewing angles?
g910.meaning: The Met suggests the wording appears to be unique. What might originality in a short blessing tell us about its maker or owner?
g910.culture: How does a pottery tradition built on calligraphy reflect the value placed on the written word in this region and period?
g910.technique: What technical challenges arise from painting with slip on a curved earthenware body and sealing it under glaze?
g910.personal: How does your own relationship to writing and handwriting affect how you respond to calligraphy as decoration?
g910.critical: How far can we interpret a design we cannot read, and what evidence would make an interpretation stronger?

g1112.daily: What does this bowl suggest about the relationship between legibility and beauty, and what evidence in the object supports your view?
g1112.emotion: How does the bowl's combination of a benevolent message and formal restraint shape its affect, even for a viewer who cannot read Arabic?
g1112.observation: Describe the bowl's design precisely, then identify where your description already begins to interpret.
g1112.analysis: Evaluate how rhythm, symmetry, and variation operate in the inscription and in the central interlace, and how the two interact.
g1112.line: How does the manipulation of vertical stroke length make line itself the subject of the design?
g1112.shape: How do the bowl's concave geometry and the radial layout together determine how the calligraphy can be seen and handled?
g1112.color: How does a limited slip palette on a pale ground construct hierarchy and mood in an object without figural imagery?
g1112.texture: What role might the contrast between the matte quality of painted slip and the slickness of glaze play in the object's visual effect?
g1112.space: How does placing a text on a curved, concave vessel complicate ideas of frontality and reading direction?
g1112.light: In what ways does a glazed surface make the object's appearance dependent on conditions of viewing?
g1112.meaning: Is a blessing on a bowl primarily a message, a talisman, or a decorative device? What evidence could support each view?
g1112.culture: What can an object made in present-day Uzbekistan and excavated in Nishapur tell us about regional networks, and what remains unknowable?
g1112.technique: How might the constraints of slip painting under glaze have encouraged the stylization of the letterforms?
g1112.personal: How does your own literacy in particular scripts shape what you notice, or fail to notice, in this bowl?
g1112.critical: The museum identifies this wording as apparently unique. How should historians weigh such claims given what survives and what has been excavated?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, medium, classification (Ceramics) and tag (Arabic) checked against the museum record, and the museum page text read: decoration is calligraphy and interlace only.

teacherNote.context: Samanid-era epigraphic pottery uses calligraphy as its principal decoration, often with blessings or proverbs. This bowl was made in present-day Uzbekistan and excavated at Nishapur in Iran.
directions: Have students design their own lettered bowl rim, stretching selected strokes to make a balanced line.
Invite students who read Arabic or other scripts to share how they would read the lettering, and discuss reading direction.
Compare this bowl with another artwork in the archive that uses pattern but no pictures.
